shapes.name: array_length
shapes.reason: An array's own length, not a caller-supplied number. A JS array cannot be longer than the safe-integer range, so the read has nothing to saturate; the budget on that length is the array-length guard's, which the shared wasmArrayLikeLength applies.

shapes.name: array_element
shapes.reason: An element read from an array whose length was taken first, indexed by the loop counter. The value is a caller-supplied number like any other, but the receiver is the element rather than a named option, so it carries no field name a range error could report; the element's own domain is checked where the struct it fills is validated.

pending_types.reason: The identifier class -- track, take, destination, parameter and clip ids, plus pitch-class and quality ordinals. Their consequence when saturated has not been measured, so they are carried rather than blessed: an id that saturates is rejected by whatever owns the id space, an ordinal that saturates may not be. Recorded as a type rather than as fifty sites so the list stays readable, and so a signed narrowing cannot hide inside it.

MIDI channel, controller and selector bytes. Same standing as the identifier class and unmeasured for the same reason; unlike it, the target type is narrow enough that a wrapped value is always in the byte domain, which is what makes the outcome worth measuring rather than assuming.

narrowings.reason: An enum ordinal switched on with a throwing default, so a saturated value is rejected rather than landing on a mode.
An enum ordinal compared against both legal values and throwing otherwise, so a saturated value has no branch to reach.
An enum ordinal range-checked against the warp-mode bounds before the cast is used, so a saturated value is refused by name.

An enum ordinal the C ABI range-checks against the curve enum's bounds, so a saturated value is refused there. The guard is in the C ABI rather than here, which is what makes this worth recording: moving the validation would make this a live narrowing again.

The shared enum reader's numeric path. It rejects a non-number before the cast but does not range-check the ordinal, so what a saturated value becomes depends on whether the patch field it fills is validated downstream. Unmeasured.
A sample rate read straight into the import request. Whether a saturated rate is refused depends on the core's rate bounds, which are not applied here. Unmeasured.
A frame position. int64_t is wide enough that a JS safe integer arrives intact, so saturation needs a value past 2^53 to reach; what the import does with an absurd start frame is unmeasured.
A time-signature numerator defaulting to 0 when absent. Whether a saturated value is refused depends on the core's time-signature validation. Unmeasured.
A time-signature denominator, under the same standing as its numerator.

A routing filter that defaults to -1 for 'no filter'. A saturated value is a filter that matches nothing rather than an error, which is the silent-empty-result outcome rather than a refusal. Unmeasured.
A routing channel filter, under the same standing as the group filter.
A remap target channel. Unlike the two filters it is written into events rather than compared against them, so a saturated value has somewhere to land. Unmeasured.
A page-provider handle. A saturated handle resolves to no provider, which is a lookup failure rather than a saturation bug -- but which of the two the engine reports is unmeasured.
A sample position on the realtime clip path. int64_t takes a JS safe integer intact; what an absurd offset does to clip scheduling is unmeasured.
A clip length, under the same standing as the clip offset.
A fade length, under the same standing as the clip offset.
A fade length, under the same standing as the clip offset.
A clip mode ordinal. Unlike the warp-mode and curve ordinals above, no range check was found beside it. Unmeasured.
The offline render length, read the same way on both the bounce and the freeze path. It drives the render loop, so an absurd value is a runtime cost rather than a wrong result. Unmeasured.

readers.reason: A default seeder rather than an options-bag reader: it turns an absent or non-numeric value into a deterministic seed, and every value in the type's range is a legal seed, so there is nothing for a range check to reject.

Delegates its narrowing to the shared checkedIntFromVal rather than casting, so the conversion contract is single-sourced and only the default-and-absence handling is local. Kept out of the shared header because its options bag is positional in a way the generic reader is not.

The float sibling of repairIntOption, and not the same defect: a float overflow produces inf, which is outside every domain and caught by any finite check, where an integer saturation produces a plausible in-domain number. Driving it found no field on its path that consumes the value, so it is unmeasured rather than benign.
An enum resolver for the pan-law ordinal, taking the string and numeric spellings together. Whether the numeric path range-checks the ordinal is unmeasured.
Reads through double rather than narrowing, so no integer cast happens here and the inline-narrowing population does not see it. It is a second numeric reader outside the shared family all the same.
The floating-point sibling of integerField, under the same standing.
An enum resolver for the sample loop mode. Unmeasured.

An enum resolver, not a size reader: the ordinal it returns is range-checked by the C ABI against the curve enum's bounds. Recorded here rather than folded into the shared family because the reader shape is incidental -- it exists to accept both the string and the numeric spelling of one enum.
The sibling enum resolver for the automation target kind. Unmeasured.

A second unsigned options-bag reader, narrowing with a bare cast and no range check -- the shape the shared int reader was fixed out of. It has no shared counterpart to delegate to, so closing it means adding an unsigned reader to the shared family, which changes behaviour on the realtime engine path.
The 64-bit sibling of uintProperty. int64_t takes a JS safe integer intact, so its exposure is narrower, but it is the same duplication.
The floating-point sibling of uintProperty. A double read cannot saturate, so this one duplicates the family without duplicating the defect.
